chunks: TL impedance vs frequency. The question: How does a TL's insertion impedance vary with respect to frequency?
"The impedance of a transmission line" can mean three different things. One is the line's own characteristic impedance, which stays about the same at high frequency.
The second is the impedance a source sees when it looks into a finite piece of line, and that changes with frequency unless the far end is matched.
The third is how much signal gets through, called insertion loss, which grows with frequency.
Picture pushing a child on a swing. Pushes in step with the swing help. Pushes out of step fight it. A mismatched line works like that.
A bounce comes back from the far end, and whether it helps or fights the outgoing signal depends on timing, so on frequency.
The source feels a different "push-back" at each frequency. With a matched end there is no bounce, so the feel never changes.
Below 100 megahertz the open line is a capacitor ( Z in about 1 over omega C' with C' equals 12 picofarads, falling with frequency).
At 415 megahertz it collapses to near a short, at 830 megahertz it spikes to an open, and it repeats.
The red lossy line shows the same pattern with the extremes softened: loss limits how deep the null and how high the peak can go, and grows with frequency.
Characteristic impedance ( Z 0 ): the resistance the line looks like to a single wave traveling along it ("Characteristic impedance explained").
Input impedance: what the source sees looking into the start of the line. It depends on the far-end load.
Matched: the far-end load equals Z 0 , so nothing bounces back ("Impedance matching: what, why, when"). Insertion loss: how much signal is lost passing through the line.
Delay: the time a wave takes to travel the length of the line.
Take a 50 ohms line with a 0. 6 nanoseconds delay. End it with a matched 50 ohms load, and the source sees 50 ohms at every frequency. Now end it with 100 ohms.
The input impedance swings between 100 ohms and 25 ohms as frequency rises, completing one swing about every 0. 83 gigahertz. That is because the bounce returns after a 1.
2 nanoseconds round trip, and 1 over 1. 2 nanoseconds about 0. 83 gigahertz. The 25 comes from 50 squared over 100 . That is the whole idea.
"I'd separate three things. The characteristic impedance is essentially constant with frequency above a few MHz, square root of L' over C' , with a small drift from loss.

The input impedance of a finite line depends on frequency through its electrical length: matched, it's Z 0 at all frequencies; unmatched, it oscillates, like an open line looking capacitive, then a short at the quarter-wave frequency, then open at the half-wave.
And insertion loss rises with frequency, roughly square root of f plus f terms, with ripples if there are reflections."
